title: A piano app that [[waits until you play it]], so you can learn a song without reading music.
hook: SoundBox is a free piano app I designed and built on my own. It lights up the keys to press, listens through the microphone, and does not move on until it hears the right notes.

facts.label: Why
facts.value: People who cannot read sheet music still want to play the songs they love

facts.label: Platform
facts.value: Android app and any web browser

facts.label: Stack
facts.value: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Capacitor, Web Audio, Basic Pitch

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Working app, version 1.1 on Android. Tested by me in a browser and an Android emulator, not yet with learners

summary: The problem: to play a song you love, you usually have to decode a page of sheet music, or keep up with a lesson that moves on whether you are ready or not.
What I built: a free app for Android and the browser. Every song comes at three levels, the keys light up on a picture of a piano, and the app listens and waits for you.
The key idea: the hard part was knowing when not to move on. Room noise, a hummed tune and a chord it cannot read must not count, so the app says “listening…” instead of guessing.
Where it stands: a working app, built in three days. There is no independent test of how well it recognises notes on real pianos, and no measured learning results.

lead.alt: The SoundBox practice screen on a laptop: Für Elise on the Simple melody level, a row of chord cards along the top, the note E shown large, and the E key lit in violet on a three-octave keyboard
lead.caption: The practice screen on a laptop, on the Simple melody level of Für Elise. The chord sheet runs along the top, the note to play is large, and its key is lit below.

sections.label: Why I built it
sections.heading: Most songs are written down for people who can read music

blocks.p: SoundBox is for someone who wants to play a song they love, well enough to sing along or to record light background music, and who cannot read sheet music.

Today that means searching the internet for the notes, finding a page of notation, and trying to work the whole page out onto the keyboard at once. A timed lesson adds a clock on top. I treated time pressure as the most discouraging thing for a beginner, and designed against it.

figures.alt: Two rows of steps. The usual way: search for notes, find sheet music you cannot read, work the page out at once, a timed lesson moves on. With SoundBox: pick the song, pick a level, see the keys lit, play and it moves on when it hears it
figures.caption: The problem in one picture. Compare the last step of each row: one clock belongs to the lesson, the other to you.

blocks.p: Before drawing any screen, I wrote down four rules the app could not break.

head: Rule
What it meant
rows: No paid services and no licensed content. Everything runs on the device.
No staff notation and no key signatures. Large type and few things on screen.
The songs and the listening all work with no network.
Readable contrast, touch targets at least 48 pixels on a touchscreen, labels for screen readers, and never colour alone.

aside.title: What I do not have.
aside.detail: I did not interview learners or watch a beginner use the app. The audience on this page comes from my own problem statement.

sections.label: How it works
sections.heading: Pick a song, pick a level, play what lights up

blocks.p: Six songs come with the app: five traditional or classical tunes and one Hindi film song. You can add your own. Each row in the library shows the key, the number of chords and how hard the easiest level is.

figures.alt: The SoundBox library on a phone: six songs in rows, each with its key, chord count and difficulty dots, and a tab bar at the bottom
figures.caption: The library on a phone. A row per song, not a card, so the facts you compare when choosing still fit.

figures.alt: The practice screen on a phone for Für Elise on Full melody: chord cards, the note E5 with D sharp next, and one lit key
figures.caption: The same piece on Full melody. The step counter reads 1 of 182, against 52 steps on Just the chords.

blocks.p: The idea that holds the product together is the song format. A song stores one set of chords and three ways to play it, from easy to hard. You start where you can and move up when the song stops being hard.

figures.alt: Diagram of three level cards, Just the chords, Simple melody and Full melody, each saying what you play and who it is for, above a band saying all three share one set of harmony
figures.caption: The three levels, in the app's own names. Read the band at the bottom: the levels are three depths of one song, not three songs.

blocks.p: Then the loop. The screen shows what to play, you play it on your own piano, and the app listens. In the default mode, called Wait for me, nothing moves until it hears the right thing.

figures.alt: Flow diagram: See, Play, Listen, Judge, then three outcomes: it matches and the song moves on, a wrong note shown in amber while the song waits, or not sure and it says listening
figures.caption: The practice loop. The third outcome matters most: when the app is unsure, it says so instead of guessing.

figures.alt: The practice screen on a phone with seven numbered notes: named header buttons, the level picker, the chord sheet, the current and next chord, the lit keys, the Listen button and the mode picker
figures.caption: The practice screen, part by part. Start at note 5: every lit key also carries a ring and a letter.

sections.label: Decision 1
sections.heading: The song waits for you, and tells you when it is unsure

blocks.p: What you see: Wait for me is the default. There is no clock. A wrong note shows in a neutral amber and the song simply stays where it is. There is no red cross and no buzzer.

When the microphone is open, a strip at the bottom says what the app is doing: “warming up…” while the detector loads, “getting used to the room…” for the first second, then “listening…” until it hears something it believes.

figures.alt: The lower half of the practice screen after pressing Listen: the C, E and A keys lit, and a strip reading listening beside a level meter and a microphone-off button
figures.caption: The listening strip after pressing Listen. I captured this in a headless browser with a simulated microphone, so it shows the waiting state, not a note being recognised.

blocks.p: In the build: the three modes, Wait for me, Play along and Hear it, share one position in the song, so switching never loses your place. Pause exists only in the timed modes. In Wait for me the player is the clock, so there is nothing to pause, and the space bar plays the current chord instead.
The listening strip names each refusal. “That sounds sung, not played” is something you can act on. Silence looks exactly like a broken microphone.
Any mode can loop a section, because nobody practises by playing a song from the top again and again. They play the eight bars they keep fumbling.

figures.alt: The practice screen on a laptop with the Opening section of Für Elise marked Looping, the other section dimmed, and a Looping Opening note under the controls
figures.caption: Looping a section. The label sits on the sheet where you are reading, as well as under the control that set it.

aside.title: The trade-off.
aside.detail: A song that waits can also get stuck, if the app fails to hear a note you played well. The skip button and the arrow keys let you move on by hand.

sections.label: Decision 2
sections.heading: It listens only for a piano, and never sends the sound anywhere

blocks.p: What you see: one Listen button, and in Settings a few plain choices. How noisy is your room? Only listen for a piano? Use a connected digital piano?

figures.alt: The Listening card in Settings: room noise choice, detector choice of Automatic, Accurate or Light, and switches for piano only, right octave and MIDI piano, each with a sentence of explanation
figures.caption: The Listening settings. Each choice carries a sentence about when to change it, written for someone who is not an engineer.

blocks.p: In the build: my first version had one check. It ignored sounds that were too quiet. Everything after that worked on a pattern with the volume taken out. A fan, a conversation or an empty room all came back looking like music, and the on-screen piano lit up end to end.
So I put five gates between the microphone and the song. Each catches a different kind of sound that is not someone playing.

figures.alt: Diagram of the listening path: microphone, then four gates for room noise, loudness, musical shape and number of notes, then the piano gate, the Basic Pitch detector, a fallback detector and matching the step
figures.caption: The path a sound takes. Gates 1 to 4 ask whether anything musical is happening. Gate 5 asks whether it came from a piano.

blocks.p: Next, I tested the chord detector against a synthesised grand piano, and it was not good enough. A chromagram, the detector's sum of sound in each of the 12 note names, cannot tell octaves apart.

head: What was played
What the first detector heard
What the model heard
rows: C2 C3 C4 E4 G4, with the octaves right
A minor 7 with the sustain pedal down
A2 A3 C4 E4 G4, with the octaves right
A melody note over a ringing chord
A C two octaves below anything played

blocks.p: A small fix solved the first two rows for the old detector. The third could not be fixed that way, so I added Basic Pitch, an open-source note-transcription model from Spotify. It has about 17,000 parameters, and its 725 KB of weights ship inside the app. The old detector stays as the fallback for phones that cannot run the model.

Then I found the app was happy to be sung to. Humming the tune moved the song on exactly as playing did. The piano gate closes that gap by looking at how a sound behaves over time: a struck string arrives at once, only gets quieter and holds its pitch. A voice fades in, holds, and wobbles.

figures.alt: Bar chart of attack scores from 0 to 1: struck string best case 1.0, struck string worst case 0.5, held voice highest seen 0.07
figures.caption: The first of the gate's three tests. The gap between 0.5 and 0.07 is the margin it works with. These figures come from synthetic sounds, not a real room.

aside.title: The trade-off.
aside.detail: The model made the live-update bundle grow from 128 KB to 818 KB, after I had cut 310 KB by dropping a component library. I accepted it, because an app whose promise is that it listens gains nothing from being small if it cannot hear a chord. It loads only on the first press of Listen.

sections.label: Decision 3
sections.heading: The keyboard gets the width, even when the phone refuses to turn

blocks.p: What you see: held upright, a phone shows two octaves that follow the notes you need. Turned sideways, the chord sheet goes and the keys fill the screen. Zen mode strips the screen down to the keys and the notes falling towards them.

figures.alt: Zen mode on a phone turned sideways with five numbered notes: the Play E instruction, the Listen and step controls, notes falling in the lane of their key, the line where notes meet the keys, and the lit E key
figures.caption: Zen mode. Note 3 is the reason it exists: the instruction arrives directly above the finger that plays it.

blocks.p: In the build: three octaves on an upright phone made each key barely wider than a fingernail. So upright phones get fewer octaves instead of smaller keys. The two-octave window stays still unless the next notes fall outside it, because a keyboard that moves every bar slides out from under the hand you are matching it to.

The Android app first shipped locked to portrait. I unlocked it, then found that many people keep auto-rotate switched off, so turning the phone did nothing. I added a sideways button that tries three routes in turn.

figures.alt: Diagram of three routes in order: ask the Android app, ask the browser, turn the page itself. The first is marked not yet watched on a device, the other two checked in the browser
figures.caption: Three ways to turn sideways. Route 3 always works, and it is the one most phones will take.

figures.alt: The practice screen on a phone turned sideways: level picker, the note E, a three-octave keyboard with E lit, and the controls in one row
figures.caption: A phone on its side. The header no longer wraps onto two lines, so that height goes to the keys.

figures.alt: Zen mode captured on an upright phone with the whole page drawn on its side, keys along the left edge
figures.caption: Route 3 caught on an upright screen: the page has turned itself. Turn the phone and it reads the right way up.

blocks.p: Zen mode only works if a falling note sits exactly over its key at every screen size. Two separate drawings would each scale on their own and drift apart at some sizes, so the keys and the notes are one drawing. Only one thing moves: the group of notes slides down as a single piece. The screen also stays awake on the practice screen, because minutes of looking without touching is exactly what a phone reads as “they have walked away”.

aside.title: The trade-off.
aside.detail: Zen mode hides the chord sheet, so you lose the shape of the song while you play. That is why it is a separate view you step into and out of, not a setting.

sections.label: Decision 4
sections.heading: Round and colourful again, but every colour has one job

blocks.p: What you see: chunky rounded buttons that sit on a darker lip and press down. Four colours, each with one meaning. Violet is the app and the note you are asked to play. Green is correct and every button that moves you forward. Amber is the streak and anything earned. Coral only ever deletes something.

figures.alt: Three phone screens side by side: the dark first version of the practice screen from 23 August, the current light version, and the current dark version
figures.caption: The practice screen on the first day and now. Compare the top right corner: a speaker icon alone at first, two named buttons now.

blocks.p: In the build: the look went round twice. My first pass had pill-shaped buttons and large flat areas of violet. I rejected it because it read like software for children. So I went square and neutral.

That stopped it looking like a toy. It also left six unlabelled icons in the practice screen's header, three filter controls in front of six songs, and option labels cut down to “Se… / Bal… / Str…”. No first-time user could read that screen.

So it went round again, on one condition: every shape and colour must carry information. Rounded corners with a lip mean you can press it. Cards have no lip, because you cannot press a card. I kept two things from the square version: a row per song in the library, and fixed-width digits so numbers do not jitter as they change.

The default theme flipped the same way. I first chose dark, for a phone on a music stand in a dim room. But most practice happens in daylight next to white keys, where a near-black screen was hard to read. Light is now the default and dark is one tap away.

figures.alt: The practice screen on a laptop with the options panel open at the bottom: microphone room setting, piano only or anything musical, and the keyboard shortcuts
figures.caption: Settings that used to crowd the screen now sit in an options panel, one tap away, each with a name.

aside.title: The trade-off.
aside.detail: A word under every icon takes room. The header keeps only two named buttons, Zen and Options, and everything else costs one extra tap.

sections.label: Decision 5
sections.heading: It keeps score, but nothing can be taken away from you

blocks.p: What you see: a daily streak, points for ground you cover, and badges. With nothing played yet, the page says “No streak yet” and how to start one.

figures.alt: The Progress screen with an amber No streak yet banner, four counters for XP earned, XP today, finished and last practised, and ten badges with one earned
figures.caption: The Progress screen as a new player sees it. The empty streak is an invitation, in amber, never a warning in red.

blocks.p: In the build: the first version refused to keep score at all, because a streak counter turns a busy fortnight into a punishment. That reason did not go away, so the scoring now follows four rules.

list: A streak survives one missed day. It breaks only after a full day with nothing played.
Points only ever go up. There is no decay, no weekly reset and no league.
Badges are for things you did, such as playing every level of one song, not for days you kept up.
Nothing is ever shown in red.

blocks.p: Points come from new ground: two for each step you had not reached before, and fifty the first time you finish a level. Your furthest point never moves back, because stepping back to drill a hard bar is the right way to practise. Points live apart from your practice history, so clearing the history does not take them away.

aside.title: What I ruled out.
aside.detail: Points for time spent. That rewards leaving the app open, and replaying a bar you already know should be worth nothing.

sections.label: Your own songs
sections.heading: An upload opens in the editor, never straight into your library

blocks.p: You can type a song bar by bar, or bring one in: a MusicXML file from MuseScore, a ChordPro file, a plain-text chord sheet, or a SoundBox export. Chords written above a line of words are matched to the syllable under them, so an imported sheet is still singable.

figures.alt: The Upload a song dialog with a drop area, a pasted chord sheet with chords above words, and a note that pictures and PDFs of sheet music cannot be read
figures.caption: A short chord sheet I typed in for this page. The grey note explains why a photo or PDF cannot be read, and what to use instead.

figures.alt: The song editor after reading the pasted sheet: a note saying 8 bars in 2 sections were read, title, key and tempo fields, and four bars each with a chord and the words under it
figures.caption: What the app made of it. Each bar kept the words that sat under its chord. Nothing is saved until you press Save.

blocks.p: In the build: importers get things wrong, and a wrong song that saved itself is worse than one you were asked to check. So every upload lands in the editor first.

Pictures and PDFs are refused with the reason. Reading notes off an image needs an online service, and nothing in this app leaves the device. A message that only says “unsupported” teaches nobody anything.

Most sheet music has no chord names, so in the last change I made the app read them back out of the notes. It weighs each note by how long it sounds, whether it falls on a strong beat and how low it is. Two limits were set by tests failing. The cost of an extra chord note had to double before a quick passing F stopped turning a G bar into G7. The confidence cut-off had to rise to 0.6 before a plain run of C, D, E, F stopped coming back as F major 7.

sections.label: The build
sections.heading: One codebase for the phone and the laptop, with the music maths tested on its own

blocks.p: The same web app runs in a browser and inside a thin Android shell. A laptop propped on the piano is a real way to use it, not an afterthought.

figures.alt: Diagram in four columns: pure music maths, sound in and out, screens and storage, and where it runs: Android app, any browser and live updates
figures.caption: How it is put together. The left column has no screens and no sound, which is what makes it testable.

head: Part
What I used
rows: Capacitor 8, a thin native shell around the web app
Web Audio for the microphone and the practice synth, Web MIDI for digital pianos
Basic Pitch on TensorFlow.js, with my own chromagram detector as the fallback
Plain CSS and a small set of controls of my own
Capgo live updates, published by GitHub Actions after the types and tests pass

blocks.p: I chose web technology for one reason: sound. Reading the microphone in real time is well documented in the browser and a chore of native code everywhere else, so I ruled out React Native and Flutter. I also started on Material UI and moved off it. It cost 310 KB in an app meant to work offline on a phone, and the practice screen is not made of Material parts. The rewrite halved the JavaScript.

stats.label: commits over three days, 23 to 25 August 2026
gates between the microphone and the song
songs that come with the app

figures.alt: Timeline of three days with commit counts: 23 August 1, 24 August 7, 25 August 2, and the main changes on each day
figures.caption: The build by day. Most of the listening work happened on 24 August, the busiest day.

blocks.p: The tests run the detection maths against synthetic piano sounds, the noise gates against synthetic room noise, and the piano gate against synthetic struck, sung, droning and sharp spoken sounds. They also check the streak across a daylight-saving change.
The hardest problems were about sound and time, not screens.

head: Problem
What went wrong, and what I changed
rows: Playing C in both hands put far more energy in C than in E and G, which then fell under the cut-off (C 1.00, E 0.41, G 0.37 against 0.56). Compressing the loud end brought back all three notes.
One low C also rings at G and E, so a simple detector reports a C major chord for a single key. The detector now damps each note's expected overtones first.
Switching level saved two progress records at the same instant, and the library offered to resume the level you had just left. A counter now breaks the tie. A unit test caught it, not my eyes.
Live updates can put new web code inside an older Android app. Every call to the native shell reports whether it worked, and each has a browser fallback.

sections.label: Accessibility
sections.heading: Sized for the device you touch, with colour never working alone

blocks.p: Sizing follows the kind of pointer, not the width of the window. With a mouse the controls are tight. On a touchscreen every target is at least 48 pixels. A narrow browser window is not a phone.

A lit key also carries a ring and its letter. Each level button has a sentence for screen readers, such as “Two chords, one per bar. Hold each one and let it ring.” When the level picker moves to its own row on a small screen, it moves rather than appearing twice, so a screen reader hears one choice and not two.

aside.title: What this does not prove.
aside.detail: These are rules I built to. I have not run an accessibility audit or a full screen-reader pass, and I do not claim one.

sections.label: Where it stands
sections.heading: It works end to end, and has not met a real learner yet

blocks.p: SoundBox works from start to finish: browse, pick a level, follow the current bar, see the next keys, let the microphone listen, and move through the song. I checked it in a browser and on an Android 14 emulator, in both themes. There is a signed Android build, version 1.1.
These things are not established:

list: There is no independent recognition benchmark. Detection is checked against synthetic piano sounds, not a real piano in a real room.
There are no measured learning results, and no beginner has used it while I watched.
The model's live path, from microphone to screen, has not yet run on real audio, and nobody has timed it on a phone.
The Android shell's own rotation and keep-awake calls have not run on a device yet.
Songs and progress stay on one device. There is no sync.

blocks.p: The screens on this page come from the browser build. The listening features need a microphone and a piano, so none of them shows a note being recognised.

sections.label: What is next
sections.heading: Test it on a real piano, then with a real beginner

list: Open “What can it hear?” in Settings on a real piano: check that the model starts, what delay it reports, and whether a two-handed chord lights the right keys.
Try the piano gate in a real room at all three noise settings.
Proposed study: watch a beginner learn one short passage in Wait for me, including how they recover when a note is missed.
Proposed benchmark: test notes and chords across rooms, microphones and pianos, and report false steps forward apart from missed notes.
Smaller features already planned: colour for left and right hand, and looping any range of bars rather than a whole section.

sections.label: What I learned
sections.heading: A patient app has to be honest about what it hears

blocks.p: I set out to remove the clock, and that part was easy. The work was in what waiting asks of the listening. A song that waits is only patient if it moves on when you play and stays when you do not. Each wrong step forward or missed note breaks the promise.

I also learned to judge a style by whether it carries information. Rounded and colourful failed once and worked the second time. The shapes stayed similar. What changed was that every corner and colour now meant something.
